meta_line: 34 bodies · 709 meetings · 4,959 located episodes over 5 routes · 302.3 audio hours transcribed · 23,237 turns scored · $17.64 of GPU time, measured 2026-10-23
lede: Nine stages, in the order they ran. Each box says what was decided at that step; the dashed ones are the two places where something is judged rather than processed. Click a box for the detail and the files behind it.

key.label: preliminary or has an open issue

money_note: Every dollar figure on this page carries the date it was measured, because these rates move: they come from the project's own spend ledger, not from a price list.

boxes.title: Meeting discovery
boxes.line: What counts as a meeting was decided by a per-body title pattern: regular sessions only, inside one twelve-month window.
boxes.detail:
Three archives, one row per body in the channel list: 402 meetings found on YouTube, 294 on Granicus and 13 on Swagit. That is 34 bodies in all: city councils, one board of supervisors and three transit boards. Metadata only at this stage: a playlist listing and an agenda page, no media.

The decision that shapes everything downstream is what a regular meeting is. Each body gets a title pattern that keeps its ordinary sessions and drops special sessions, study sessions and committees, and the window runs 2025-09-20 to 2026-09-20 and is closed. That gives 2,412.4 hours of video as the frame. Bodies whose archive could not be located at all are a known selection limit and are listed in the plan, not silently dropped.

boxes.title: Download and transcode
boxes.line: How fast this runs was decided by YouTube, not by this project: a few requests at a time from one Mac, and a bot check stops the worker rather than retrying.
boxes.detail:
Captions come first and cost nothing. The platform caption tracks are YouTube auto-captions, Granicus VTT and Swagit transcripts. They are fetched slowly by a background worker, and they decide where to look before any audio is pulled. Only then is audio downloaded and cut to the located spans, two or three at a time, from this one machine.

The constraint is a daily YouTube budget that this project does not set. A “confirm you’re not a bot” page or an HTTP 429 stops the downloader and pages the owner; nothing retries in a loop, and no personal account cookies are ever used. 5 clips are cut or queued and waiting for their turn, which is why some bodies' hours are floors rather than totals.

boxes.title: Locate: which stretches are about the topic
boxes.line: Decided twice over, by two routes with measured recall: a keyword screen with an LLM behind it, and whole-meeting transcription read with no screen at all.
boxes.detail:
Route one, the cheap one. Caption windows are scored against keyword lists, the candidates go to an LLM with a pinned codebook, and it decides whether each window is about housing density, about transit, both, a passing mention or nothing. Adjacent “about” windows merge into an episode. Its measured recall is a share of the reference's about-minutes: 0.725 on any topic and 0.304 on transit. The leak is almost entirely the keyword screen in front of the model, not the model: fare becomes fair, ridership becomes wrership, YIMBY and rezoning drop out of the captions altogether.

Route two, the expensive one. For the bodies whose audio is not on YouTube, every regular meeting is transcribed whole, undiarized, and then read on every 120-second window with no keyword screen at all. Recall there is 0.898 on any topic and 0.919 on transit, on the same share of about-minutes. Transcribing a meeting whole and undiarized is the cheap part of that, at $0.0093, measured 2026-10-20, which is why it was worth doing for half the corpus.

Route is kept as a stratum in every model and nothing is pooled across routes, because the routes that read the same body can disagree about it. 815 screened and 612 whole-meeting episodes are past the QA gate. The recall figures are measured against a reference the newer codebook itself partly defined, so they are a best case rather than an estimate.

The reading itself, every window either route sent to the model on both arms, comes to $61.33, measured 2026-10-25.

boxes.title: GPU transcription with diarization
boxes.line: Nothing starts until the owner approves that batch: the estimate is written first, the pod only runs after a yes, and it is torn down after.
boxes.detail:
Clip audio is batched on the Mac with a cost estimate attached; the owner approves the batch; only then does a pod start. It runs WhisperX large-v3 with pyannote/speaker-diarization-community-1, so the output is not just words but words attributed to separate voices. It uploads one JSON per episode and is torn down. An orphan-pod check pages the owner if anything is still billing with no batch running.

Measured rather than estimated: $0.0218, measured 2026-10-23 with diarization on, over 366.4 audio-hours in 23 finished batches, $7.97, measured 2026-10-23 in all. Every GPU pod this project has ever run comes to $17.64, measured 2026-10-23. Dropping diarization roughly halves the rate, to $0.0093, measured 2026-10-20, which is what the whole-meeting route in step 3 does.

The estimate is frozen onto the batch row when it is written, so a later measured throughput does not rewrite what was approved.

boxes.title: QA gate: whether the transcript holds up
boxes.line: A transcript is compared with the caption track for the same span, and a failing one is never loaded rather than being loaded with a warning.
boxes.detail:
Every transcript is checked against the captions for the same span, for coverage gaps, duplicated segments and diarization collapse. 1,692 episodes pass, 149 carry a warning and 0 fail. A failing transcript is never loaded: the row is requeued instead, which is the one loop in this chart.

Whole meetings need one special case. A long recording trips the repeated-phrase rule on runs of “you” and “Thank you.” across a recess, which is silence rather than a decoder loop, so those are re-gated with filler runs collapsed. A genuine coverage failure stays failed.

What came through the gate is 30,880 turns and 2,467,139 words of speech. Names are kept, by owner decision: these are public meetings and every turn on the dashboard links to the recording at its own timestamp.

boxes.title: Turn-level stance coding, each turn read three times
boxes.line: Reliability was decided by reading every turn three times and keeping the median. That measures the instrument against itself, not against a human.
boxes.detail:
Every turn of at least five words inside a located episode is coded for stance toward the agenda item. Stance runs on a scale from −2 for opposing it to +2 for supporting it. The same read scores hostility on a scale from 0 to 4, a frame set, a sub-topic and whether the speaker said who they are. The codebook is hashed into the prompt version recorded on every row, thinking is disabled, and each turn is read three times with the median kept and the spread stored. This is a census of the gated corpus, not a sample: 2,003 turns in 942 episodes.

The three readings agree at weighted κ 0.980 / 0.982 / 0.979, one value per pair of readings. Weighted κ runs from 0, the agreement chance would give, to 1, perfect agreement. The three readings are identical on 97.6 % of turns. That is the instrument agreeing with itself. No human has coded any turn, so the κ ≥ 0.6 validity gate is unpassed and everything downstream of here is exploratory. That is the single most important sentence on this page.

Cost: $96.60, measured 2026-10-25 for the pass, $0.00416, measured 2026-10-25 per turn, read three times.

boxes.title: Role audit: public or dais
boxes.line: Who counts as the public was decided by what a speaker says about themselves, which overrides the cue-phrase label it started with.
nums: no signal, share of all turns
boxes.detail:
Roles start from cue phrases in the diarized transcript, “my name is, I live at” against “the motion carries”, never from names. That labeller assigns the wrong role often enough to matter: a council member who chairs an item can pick up a public cue, and a staff planner presenting a report matches neither cue set. So the role is re-decided from what the speaker says about who they are, and that overrides the cue.

Of 12,560 turns that say anything about the speaker, 913 disagree with the cue label (7.3 % of those turns); 45.9 % of all turns say nothing and keep the cue. The audit moves clusters both ways, so a shift in these numbers is a re-partition and not contamination removed.

This is an audit, not a gold set. The self-identification is another model's output and no human has checked it, so the audited public bucket is still mixed at an unknown rate.

boxes.title: Speaker clusters, and a label for each
boxes.line: A speaker is one diarized voice inside one meeting and nothing wider: clusters are never linked across meetings, by design.
boxes.detail:
The turn scores are rolled up per diarized voice per episode. A cluster is YIMBY if its mean stance is at or above +0.50, and NIMBY if at or below −0.50. Between the two it is neutral, which is half a codebook step either side. Housing, transit and mixed episodes all carry the label since the direction pass went in on 2026-10-24: the sign on each statement follows whether its proposal would add or restrict housing or transit, so the label is support for more of either.

A cluster is a voice in one meeting, not a person. There are no voice embeddings, no persistent speaker ids and no name extraction into a field, so a cluster label means nothing outside its own episode. The same person at two meetings is two clusters, and the analysis cannot tell. Most public clusters rest on a single scored turn, which is why the per-body intervals are wide and why one table and one figure exist per locate route, never pooled.

boxes.title: The nested mixed model
boxes.line: The grouping was decided by the data: turns nest inside stretches of meeting, inside meetings, inside the bodies that held them.
nums: times the odds, public vs dais: took a side at all
boxes.detail:
One row per scored turn. The fit is a mixed logistic regression that gives every stretch of meeting, every meeting and every body its own baseline. Speaker role, renter share, their interaction and the locate route are fixed terms. The outcome is whether a turn took a side at all rather than scoring inside the neutral band.

Took a side at all: 8.20× the odds of taking a side, for a public statement against a dais one (likely range 6.46 to 10.51).

A statement took a side when its corrected stance score was 0.5 or more away from neutral. The scale runs from -2 for opposing more housing or transit to +2 for supporting more of it.

The model groups turns by meeting rather than by city because meeting is nested inside body and absorbs most of the spread between bodies. Section 5 gives that spread at each level, for each step. Earlier fits grouped by body, which is the wrong level; they are kept in the repo and agree with this one to within a few thousandths of a log-odds. The role block on the dashboard reports this model and nothing else.
